title: Häsichenbraut
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 66. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). The tale is printed entirely in dialect, with Grimm’s own parenthetical glosses of the dialect words preserved (Hersche (Hirse), fresch (frisch, lustig)); 1857 spelling preserved (daß, frißt).
about: KHM 66, one of the shortest tales in the collection and among the strangest. A hare in the cabbage patch carries a girl off on his tail to be married, and the wedding is held under a rainbow with a crow for parson and a fox for sexton; the bride escapes by leaving a straw doll in her own clothes at the millet pot. It is told in Low German from beginning to end, apart from one aside in which the teller steps out of the story to say who the guests were — and Grimm glosses two dialect words (Hersche, fresch) in parentheses in the 1857 text, which we keep.

sentences.t: Et was ene Frou mit ener Toachter in änen schöhnen Goarten mit Koal; dahin kam än Häsichen und froaß zo Wenterszit allen Koal.
sentences.l: There was a woman with a daughter in a fine garden with cabbage; thither came a little hare and ate up all the cabbage in the wintertime.
sentences.i: There was once a woman with a daughter, and a fine garden of cabbages; and there came a little hare that ate up all the cabbage in the wintertime.
sentences.n: This tale is told in Low German throughout, and every line of it will look a little foreign even to a reader at home in the standard language. Et was = es war; ene Frou = eine Frau; ener Toachter = einer Tochter; änen schöhnen Goarten = einen schönen Garten; Koal = Kohl; froaß = fraß (fressen, used of animals); zo Wenterszit = zur Winterszeit. Häsichen is the diminutive of Hase — modern Häschen, a little hare.

sentences.t: Da seit de Frou zur Toachter „gäh in den Goarten, und jags Häsichen.“
sentences.l: Then says the woman to the daughter “go into the garden, and chase the little-hare away.”
sentences.i: Then the woman said to her daughter: “Go into the garden and drive the hare off.”
sentences.n: seit = sagt; de Frou = die Frau; gäh = geh; jags = jag ’s, that is jage das (Häsichen), with the article swallowed onto the verb. From here the tale tells itself almost entirely in the present tense, which is why the German verbs stay present while the English idiom settles into the past.

sentences.t: Seits Mäken zum Häsichen „schu! schu! du Häsichen, frißt noch allen Koal.“
sentences.l: Says the girl to the little-hare “shoo! shoo! you little-hare, you eat up all the cabbage yet.”
sentences.i: The girl said to the hare: “Shoo! Shoo, you hare — you will eat up all the cabbage!”
sentences.n: Seits is seit ’s — the verb with the neuter article das clitic onto it: “says the girl.” Both Mäken (Mädchen) and Häsichen are diminutives and therefore neuter, and you will meet kummts and brachts built the same way. noch here means “at this rate, in the end.”

sentences.t: Seits Häsichen „kumm, Mäken, und sett dich uf min Haosenschwänzeken und kumm mit in min Haosenhüttchen.“
sentences.l: Says the little-hare “come, girl, sit yourself on my little-hare’s-tail and come with me into my little-hare’s-hut.”
sentences.i: The hare said: “Come, girl, sit down on my little hare’s tail and come with me into my little hare’s hut.”
sentences.n: uf = auf, min = mein. Haosenschwänzeken and Haosenhüttchen are both diminutives — the hare’s little tail and his little hut. A hare’s tail is a tuft the size of a thumb, so the invitation is absurd before it is sinister.

sentences.t: Mäken well nech.
sentences.l: The girl will not.
sentences.i: The girl would not.
sentences.n: well = will (wollen), nech = nicht. Three words, and no reason given.

sentences.t: Am annern Tog kummts Häsichen weder und frißt den Koal, do seit de Frou zur Toachter „gäh in den Goarten, und jags Häsichen.“
sentences.l: On the other day the little-hare comes again and eats the cabbage; then says the woman to the daughter “go into the garden, and chase the little-hare away.”
sentences.i: The next day the hare came again and ate the cabbage, and the woman said to her daughter: “Go into the garden and drive the hare off.”
sentences.n: annern = andern, Tog = Tag, weder = wieder. “am andern Tag” = the next day.

sentences.t: Seits Mäken zum Häsichen „schu! schu! du Häsichen, frißt noch allen Koal.“
sentences.l: Says the girl to the little-hare “shoo! shoo! you little-hare, you eat up all the cabbage yet.”
sentences.i: The girl said to the hare: “Shoo! Shoo, you hare — you will eat up all the cabbage!”
sentences.n: In “du Häsichen, frißt noch allen Koal” the subject du drops away before the second-person verb frißt (fressen) — the line scolds rather than states.

sentences.t: Seits Häsichen „kumm, Mäken, sett dich uf min Haosenschwänzeken und kumm mit mer in min Haosenhüttchen.“
sentences.l: Says the little-hare “come, girl, sit yourself on my little-hare’s-tail and come with me into my little-hare’s-hut.”
sentences.i: The hare said: “Come, girl, sit down on my little hare’s tail and come with me into my little hare’s hut.”
sentences.n: mer = mir (dative), as med stands for mit below. This time the hare says “kumm mit mer,” where the first invitation was only “kumm mit.”

sentences.t: Mäken well nech.
sentences.l: The girl will not.
sentences.i: The girl would not.

sentences.t: Am dretten Tog kummts Häsichen weder und frißt den Koal.
sentences.l: On the third day the little-hare comes again and eats the cabbage.
sentences.n: dretten = dritten. The three approaches repeat almost word for word, with a small slip each time.

sentences.t: Do seit de Frou zur Toachter „gäh in den Goarten und jags Häsichen.“
sentences.l: Then says the woman to the daughter “go into the garden, and chase the little-hare away.”
sentences.i: Then the woman said to her daughter: “Go into the garden and drive the hare off.”
sentences.n: Do = da (then), spelled with an o here and with an a in the mother’s first command: the dialect spelling is not fixed.

sentences.t: Seits Mäken „schu! schu! du Häsichen, frißt noch allen Koal.“
sentences.l: Says the girl “shoo! shoo! you little-hare, you eat up all the cabbage yet.”
sentences.i: The girl said: “Shoo! Shoo, you hare — you will eat up all the cabbage!”
sentences.n: The third time she does not even address him: zum Häsichen has dropped out.

sentences.t: Seits Häsichen „kumm, Mäken, sett dich uf min Haosenschwänzeken und kumm mit mer in min Haosenhüttchen.“
sentences.l: Says the little-hare “come, girl, sit yourself on my little-hare’s-tail and come with me into my little-hare’s-hut.”
sentences.i: The hare said: “Come, girl, sit down on my little hare’s tail and come with me into my little hare’s hut.”

sentences.t: Mäken sätzt sich uf den Haosenschwänzeken, do brachts Häsichen weit raus in sin Hüttchen und seit „nu koach Grinkoal und Hersche (Hirse), ick well de Hochtidlüd beten.“
sentences.l: The girl sets herself on the little-hare’s-tail, then the little-hare carried her far out into his little hut and says “now cook kale and millet, I will invite the wedding-folk.”
sentences.i: The girl sat down on the hare’s little tail, and the hare carried her far away to his hut and said: “Now cook kale and millet — I am going to bid the wedding guests.”
sentences.n: sätzt = setzt; brachts = brachte ’s, “the little hare brought”; sin = sein; nu koach = nun koch; Grinkoal = Grünkohl, curly kale; ick well = ich will; beten = bitten, here to invite. Grimm glosses Hersche himself in the 1857 text as Hirse, millet. Nothing is said of her consent: she sits down, and she is a bride.

sentences.t: Do kamen alle Hochtidlüd zusam’m.
sentences.l: Then came all the wedding-folk together.
sentences.i: Then all the wedding guests gathered.
sentences.n: Hochtidlüd = Hochzeitsleute; Low German Lüd = Leute, folk, and Hochtid = Hochzeit. zusam’m is zusammen with the middle swallowed, as it is spoken.

sentences.t: (Wer waren dann die Hochzeitsleute?
sentences.l: (Who then were the wedding-folk?
sentences.n: The aside steps out of dialect into standard German — the teller in her own voice, breaking off to answer a question no one asked. dann here is denn, the flavouring particle: “well now, who were they?”

sentences.t: das kann ich dir sagen, wie mirs ein anderer erzählt hat: das waren alle Hasen, und die Krähe war als Pfarrer dabei, die Brautleute zu trauen, und der Fuchs als Küster, und der Altar war unterm Regenbogen).
sentences.l: that I can tell you, as another told it to me: those were all hares, and the crow was there as parson, to marry the bridal-pair, and the fox as sexton, and the altar was under the rainbow).
sentences.i: I can tell you that, just as another told it to me: they were all hares, and the crow was there as the parson, to marry the couple, and the fox as sexton, and the altar stood under the rainbow.)
sentences.n: trauen is the technical verb for performing a marriage. A Küster is the sexton or parish clerk who assists at the service. The whole picture arrives at second hand — the teller reports another teller, and Grimm keeps the report as a report.

sentences.t: Mäken aober was trurig, da se so alleene was.
sentences.l: The girl however was sad, since she was so alone.
sentences.i: But the girl was sad, being so alone.
sentences.n: aober = aber, trurig = traurig, da se so alleene was = da sie so allein war. da here means “since, because.” The pronoun se is feminine though Mäken is grammatically neuter: the sense wins.

sentences.t: Kummts Häsichen und seit „thu uf, thu uf, de Hochtidlüt senn fresch (frisch, lustig).“
sentences.l: Comes the little-hare and says “open up, open up, the wedding-folk are merry.”
sentences.i: The hare came and said: “Open up, open up — the wedding guests are merry.”
sentences.n: “thu uf” = tu auf, open up. senn = sind. Grimm supplies the gloss for fresch in the 1857 text himself — not “fresh” but frisch, lustig: lively, in high spirits.

sentences.t: De Braut seit nischt und wint.
sentences.l: The bride says nothing and weeps.
sentences.n: nischt = nichts, wint = weint. She is de Braut now, the bride; the tale confers the title without ever having asked her.

sentences.t: Häsichen gäht fort, Häsichen kummt weder und seit „thu uf, thu uf, de Hochtidlüt senn hongrig.“
sentences.l: The little-hare goes away, the little-hare comes again and says “open up, open up, the wedding-folk are hungry.”
sentences.i: The hare went away, and came back, and said: “Open up, open up — the wedding guests are hungry.”
sentences.n: gäht = geht; hongrig = hungrig.

sentences.t: De Braut seit weder nischt und wint.
sentences.l: The bride again says nothing and weeps.

sentences.t: Häsichen gäht fort, Häsichen kummt und seit „thu uf, thu uf, de Hochtidlüt waorten.“
sentences.l: The little-hare goes away, the little-hare comes and says “open up, open up, the wedding-folk are waiting.”
sentences.i: The hare went away, and came, and said: “Open up, open up — the wedding guests are waiting.”
sentences.n: waorten = warten. Three demands, each one barer than the last: merry, hungry, waiting.

sentences.t: Do seit de Braut nischt und Häsichen gäht fort, aober se macht ene Puppen von Stroah met eren Kleedern, und giebt er eenen Röhrleppel, und set se an den Kessel med Hersche, und gäht zor Motter.
sentences.l: Then the bride says nothing and the little-hare goes away, but she makes a doll of straw with her clothes, and gives her a stirring-spoon, and sets her at the kettle with millet, and goes to her mother.
sentences.i: This time the bride said nothing, and the hare went off; but she made a doll of straw and dressed it in her own clothes, gave it a stirring spoon and set it by the kettle of millet, and went home to her mother.
sentences.n: met eren Kleedern = mit ihren Kleidern; giebt er = gibt ihr (the dative “to her”); Röhrleppel = Rührlöffel, a stirring spoon; set se = setzt sie; med = mit; zor Motter = zur Mutter. The doll wears the bride’s own clothes, which is the whole of the trick.

sentences.t: Häsichen kummt noch ämahl und seit „thu uf, thu uf,“ und macht uf und smet de Puppe an Kopp, daß er de Hube abfällt.
sentences.l: The little-hare comes once more and says “open up, open up,” and opens up and strikes the doll on the head, so that the cap falls off her.
sentences.i: The hare came once more and said, “Open up, open up,” and opened the door himself, and struck the doll on the head, so that its cap fell off.
sentences.n: smet = schmeißt (schmeißen, to fling); an Kopp = an den Kopf. In “daß er de Hube abfällt,” er is the dative ihr — the cap falls off her, a dative of possession in dialect spelling. Die Hube (Haube) is the married woman’s cap: knocking it off is what shows the head beneath to be straw.

sentences.t: Do set Häsichen daß sine Braut nech es und gäht fort und es trurig.
sentences.l: Then the little-hare sees that it is not his bride and goes away and is sad.
sentences.i: Then the hare saw that it was not his bride, and went away, and was sad.
sentences.n: set = sieht; sine = seine; nech es = nicht ist — es here is the verb “is,” not the pronoun “it,” which is the one form in this dialect most likely to trip a reader. The tale stops there: nothing is said of the girl, nothing is resolved, and the last word belongs to the hare’s sadness.
